mappings.note: Assertion-reason tying atman's identity with brahman to the interdependence of all beings - a doctrinal inference, so LO-150. Not LO-136, no text's contents are at issue.
Finds the false gloss (moksha as the cycle of rebirth rather than release from it) across ritam, karma and dharma; the whole item is technical vocabulary of ancient thought.
Places a described seeker's aims within Upanishadic and Vedantic thought against Charvaka, ritualist and Stoic distractors - identifying a school by its ideas, so LO-150.
The Shvetaketu and Uddalaka dialogue located in the Upanishads: a text-identification demand (LO-136) about a brahman teaching (LO-150).
'Raja' as the ruler of a jana - early Vedic political organisation, which belongs with the janas and sabha items under LO-138. Not LO-144, whose government is present-day and local.
Charvaka materialism and its failure to endure; the reason states the school's tenets, so this is an analysis of an ancient system of thought.
Agni as the fire deity receiving daily offerings - a fact about Vedic religious practice, hence LO-150 rather than a textual outcome.
Defines the monk or nun who renounces worldly life for a monastic order - the institutional form these ancient traditions took, so LO-150.
Toda reverence for particular Nilgiri peaks: a named tribal community (LO-141) and its belief system (LO-150).
Defines 'spiritual' as pertaining to the inner soul rather than material concerns - the conceptual vocabulary the chapter's systems of thought rest on.
Rejects ritam as 'poetic meter' among ahimsa, karma and brahman pairings; again discrimination among doctrinal terms and their schools.

'Janjati' as the constitutional term for tribal communities - naming a form of India's human diversity, which is LO-141. Not CG-SST3, since no constitutional value or process is at issue, only the word used.
The Rig Veda as the oldest of the four - a fact about the body of ancient literature, so LO-136 rather than the doctrine outcome.
'Bhikshu' as a fully ordained monk of the Sangha; the organisation of the Buddhist community, under LO-150.
A community's annual rites at a mountain read as belief in nature's sacredness - a value of a folk or tribal system of thought (LO-150) held by a distinct community (LO-141).
The rigour of oral transmission and the fidelity it produced: a claim about how the Vedic texts survived, which is a fact about the works rather than about their doctrine.
Spots 'ritam - material possessions (Jainism)' as false, which needs both the Vedic sense of ritam and the Jain aparigraha; term-to-school discrimination, so LO-150.
Vedic chanting as INTANGIBLE heritage - the recognition of an Indian cultural contribution, which LO-149 names. Mapped with the other UNESCO items rather than with the text items.
Aham brahmasmi pointing to the divine nature within; a core Upanishadic doctrine, so LO-150.
'Veda' as knowledge - the short-answer twin of the etymology item, and like it a fact about the texts.
Names the Rig Veda as the most ancient; recall about the body of ancient literature, so LO-136.
Where the hymns were composed: a fact about the texts (LO-136) anchored on the Sapta Sindhava river country (LO-132).
Rishis and rishikas as the composers - authorship of the literary works, hence LO-136.
Ritam as cosmic and human order; a Vedic concept, so LO-150 rather than a fact about the text.
Janas as the clans of early Vedic society - ancient social organisation, mapped with the raja and sabha items.
Sabha or samiti as a collective assembly; early governance in the ancient period, so LO-138.
Yajna as the ritual offering to deities - Vedic religious practice, under LO-150 with the Agni item.
Brahman as Vedanta's one divine essence; the short-answer twin of the multiple-choice version, and again a doctrine.
Translates aham brahmasmi - the meaning of a central Upanishadic statement, so LO-150.
Lumbini as the Buddha's birthplace. LO-135 is withheld because Lumbini is in Nepal and that outcome asks for sites on the map of India.
'Buddha' as the awakened one; the meaning of the title, and so of the attainment the tradition rests on.
Ahimsa translated as non-violence - a shared value of these traditions, the values clause of LO-150.
The Sangha as the order of monks and nuns the Buddha founded; the institutional form of the tradition.
Mahavira's birth into a Kshatriya royal family - a biographical fact about the founder of Jainism, so LO-150.
'Jina' as conqueror of ignorance and attachment; the idea the name Jain carries.
Anekantavada as the manifoldness of truth - a distinctive Jain doctrine, hence LO-150.
Aparigraha as non-possession; the companion Jain principle to anekantavada, under the same outcome.
What the 2008 UNESCO listing signifies for Vedic chanting - India's cultural contribution receiving world recognition, so LO-149.
The rishis' view that the many deities are one reality, at short-answer length; a doctrinal claim, so LO-150.
Explains atman as the Self one with brahman - the Upanishadic doctrine, mapped like the multiple-choice version.
